title: Xiaomi's Three-Chip Gambit: Buying Time with Resources, Betting on an On-Device AI Paradigm Shift
dek: Xiaomi releases three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture, trading resources for time in a bet on an on-device AI paradigm shift and vertical integration—but it still trails top-tier chip companies by a clear margin.
why: This episode offers a deep dive into the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips. It's dense with information, with clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking—worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors tracking Xiaomi.
who: Investors focused on Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals wanting to understand on-device AI trends.
skip: The first 3 minutes discussing the definition of self-developed chips can be skipped; jump straight to the technical analysis.

points.h: Whether a company can make chips depends on system definition power, not IP self-development rate
points.body: To judge whether a company can really make chips, you can't just look at how many IP blocks it hand-crafted; you need to see how much system definition power it holds. Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, but system integration and physical implementation are its own. Apple and Qualcomm excel at iterating yearly and continuously taping out—something latecomers lack most. Xiaomi doesn't have a decade to learn slowly, so it chooses an aggressive path, advancing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

points.h: The culprit behind O1's poor energy efficiency is a missing shared water tank
points.body: The Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), causing power consumption to spike under heavy GPU load and hurting energy efficiency. An SLC is like a shared water tank in a residential complex: the closer data is to the compute units, the faster the access and the lower the power. The O1 has many GPU cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores sit idle waiting for data—that's the bandwidth wall. The O3 adds a 16MB SLC, splits it into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduling system to handle data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's off-the-shelf bus is too generic, so Xuanjie had to build its own
points.body: ARM's standard CHI+CMN solution is too generic; it must retain compatibility and redundancy, making it hard to tailor for Xuanjie. The O3 instead develops its own X-Ring unified fabric, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, along with a custom high-speed network hub and memory controller. This reduces protocol conversion overhead and lets data decide cache placement and paths based on demand. Xiaomi claims protocol conversion overhead drops 75%, and static access latency is 82 nanoseconds—32% lower than the O1 and even lower than Apple's A19 Pro.

points.h: The compute bottleneck is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations
points.body: The O3 adds AI units to every subsystem—CPU, GPU, ISP, etc.—so computation happens where the data resides, reducing data movement. The NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200 TOPS, because Xiaomi judges that the bottleneck for large models is expanding from matrix multiplication to vector operations like Softmax, quantization, and KV cache. The vector unit area is comparable to the Tensor unit, with 6.8 times the multiply-accumulate units of the O1, and it introduces an SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be co-defined by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no accuracy loss, cutting memory bandwidth and capacity needs by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model runs on the O3, with prefill performance up 40% and decode up 45%. This ability to co-define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration—no need to wait for others to define a model and then adapt a generic chip.

points.h: 3nm performance is squeezed out cell by cell with standard cells
points.body: The O3 uses the more mature N3P process, delivering 5% better performance at the same power and 5%-10% lower power at the same frequency. Xiaomi also did extensive process optimization: self-developed standard cells grew from 480 in the O1 to over 2,400, covering various chip units; it compressed the power-supply buffer channels so power and signals route from the middle of modules, boosting transistor density by 5%. The CPU went from a 4-cluster to a 3-cluster 10-core all-big-core design, with single-core performance up 31% and multi-core up 60%, surpassing the A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: The Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer plus two memory wafers stacked vertically, connected via hybrid bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical interconnects to achieve high bandwidth with lower energy per bit shift—like an HBM for phones. Data: 28,762 data connections, 1.22TB/s bandwidth, far exceeding the tens-of-bits-wide connection of a traditional SoC with LPDDR. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each paired with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: CXMT's value isn't in speed grades but in co-definition
points.body: Xiaomi partners with CXMT to debut LPDDR6, reducing reliance on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if CXMT offers the 10.667Gbps entry-level grade, Xiaomi can compensate for peak rate gaps with wider channels, larger SLC, and a custom memory controller. More importantly, the two co-validate and tune from the design stage, jointly defining a Chinese mobile memory subsystem solution. For CXMT, this proves its high-speed I/O and physical layer capabilities, earning a seat at the next-generation mobile memory table.

points.h: What Xiaomi is betting on isn't chips—it's a time window
points.body: First, it bets on a paradigm shift in on-device computing, where AI's weight in the SoC grows and phones become the entry point for AI interaction—Xiaomi wants to stand in the definer's position. Second, it bets that vertical integration becomes a core competitive advantage for device companies; generic chips can't meet the fragmented needs of the human-car-home ecosystem, so you must own your compute architecture. Third, it bets on an uncertain time window, trading resources for time to compress the catch-up cycle, preferring to bear engineering risk rather than wait for the window to close.

points.h: Xuanjie is catching up faster, but it hasn't cleared any of the three thresholds
points.body: Top-tier SoC companies need three capabilities: self-developed CPU/GPU microarchitecture, self-developed 5G baseband, and continuous multi-generation tape-outs with tens of millions of shipments. Xuanjie currently meets none of these, still clearly trailing the first tier—it's just catching up faster. What truly reshapes the industry isn't a single stunning chip but the sustained iteration capability built by a group of companies. Xuanjie's larger significance is proving Xiaomi's chip efforts haven't stopped and that it's moving forward with Chinese chip industry partners.

terms.def: A cache shared by multiple compute units within a chip, like a shared water tank in a residential complex.
A wafer-level 3D stacking interconnect technology that uses direct copper-to-copper connections for high bandwidth and low power.
Placing memory and compute units close together to reduce data movement distance, improving bandwidth and energy efficiency.
A performance bottleneck where data movement capability becomes the limiting factor, so adding more compute cores doesn't help.
A parallel processing architecture that can manage multiple task groups at once, improving utilization of compute units.
